@SP tl;dr can just be a reply to a long block of text (too long; didn’t read) but it can also be used, often by the person who is posting the long block of text, to be a heading for a summary of that long block of text.

This is the kind of thing you might see:

Subject: should I move to another country?

tl;dr: my wife has been offered a new job in Thailand but I am scared of flying 

Hi folks, I’ve been here on this forum for a long time and I always appreciate your advice. I wonder if you can help me figure out the pros and cons of my situation. Basically I’ve been scared of airplanes since I was 8 years old, when I somehow got the idea that Leslie Nielsen had given everyone on that plane food poisoning deliberately. It actually affected me more than just with airplanes. I’m now also terrified of bumbling police detectives and all men who might be described as silver foxes. I’m sorry you didn’t find the Tricky Clues section helpful today! Selecting the Tricky Clues can be ... tricky. Like crosswords as a whole, a clue’s difficulty is very subjective; one solver’s gimme is another’s stumper. I generally try to select question-marked clues that require a logical leap, misdirectors, neologisms that some folks may not have heard yet (see: REKT), or more deep-cut, “know it or you don’t” trivia. I also try to pick clues from different parts of the puzzle, for solvers who might be stuck in a particular corner or quadrant and need a toehold. And unless it solves to a real ten-dollar word, synonym-style clues don’t always lend themselves to a meaty explanation or teach a broader solving skill — there’s not much else to say about the connection between [Puppy] and WHELP, other than that WHELP is another word for puppy. 

Still, I understand the frustration when a clue that you want an explanation for doesn’t appear in the Tricky Clues section! I just wanted to provide a little insight into how I choose them. I hope that next one is more helpful.
